TP63 is the transcriptional regulator here, and in the absence of any repression mechanism the default regulatory relationship is activation: p63 binds the promoter/enhancer of its target and drives its transcription. L3HYPDH (trans-3-hydroxy-L-proline dehydratase, a proline-catabolism enzyme) therefore sits downstream as a positively controlled target. The causal order is: TP63 protein is lost or reduced → occupancy of the L3HYPDH regulatory element drops → the activating signal at that promoter falls → L3HYPDH mRNA (and subsequently protein) declines relative to the matched unperturbed control. Rise would only be expected if TP63 were acting as a repressor (i.e., if loss relieved direct repression, or if loss triggered a compensatory pathway that secondarily induced L3HYPDH), and no such mechanism is specified for this pair; the straightforward activator-loss logic gives down.

TET2 is a 5-methylcytosine dioxygenase whose loss removes the 5hmC intermediate needed for both passive and TDG/BER-dependent active demethylation, so the DNA methylation it normally keeps off regulatory elements accumulates. Two convergent branches push WIPF1 transcription downward. First, TET2 loss drives progressive hypermethylation of active enhancers and estrogen response elements; the resulting 5mC recruits MBD/MeCP2-HDAC complexes, compacts chromatin, and — because TET2 also recruits OGT to maintain HCF1-SET1/COMPASS-dependent H3K4me3 — strips the activating mark that keeps these elements competent, so ERα occupancy at its response elements is impaired and the ERα-driven transcriptional output falls. Second, TET2 in complex with FOXP1 maintains demethylation of ESR1 itself, so its loss additionally lowers ESR1 expression and hence the abundance of the very activator that drives WIPF1. Since ESR1 acts as an activator of the WIPF1-coexpressed module, the order is: TET2 loss → 5hmC loss and enhancer/promoter hypermethylation (plus reduced H3K4me3) → weakened ESR1 expression and ERα binding at its target elements → reduced transcription of ESR1-dependent targets including WIPF1. Down is therefore the expected direction, though the effect should be modest and locus-dependent, since TET2 loss fine-tunes rather than abolishes ERα target transcription.

GATA1 is the master erythroid transcription factor that directly occupies and activates the erythroid promoter/enhancer of Slc4a1 (Band 3/AE1), so Slc4a1 transcription is a readout of functional GATA1 dosage. The D218G substitution sits in the N-terminal zinc finger and impairs GATA1's DNA-binding/cofactor (FOG1) engagement, producing a hypomorphic, loss-of-function allele (the X-linked dyserythropoietic anemia with thrombocytopenia phenotype). With a crippled activator bound at the Slc4a1 regulatory region, the causal order is: variant → reduced GATA1 transactivation capacity (key mediator: GATA1 itself, acting as the sequence-specific activator at the Slc4a1 locus) → less RNA polymerase II recruitment → lower Slc4a1 mRNA. Hence, relative to matched unperturbed control in the same context, Slc4a1 expression is expected to go down.

miR-210 is a hypoxia-induced microRNA whose canonical, well-validated target is the iron–sulfur cluster assembly scaffold ISCU. Gaining miR-210 activity loads the RISC/Argonaute2 complex with a guide strand bearing a seed match in the ISCU 3′UTR; pairing there first causes translational repression and then accelerated deadenylation and decay of the ISCU transcript, so within the same hypoxic context the perturbed cells end up with less ISCU mRNA and protein than the matched unperturbed control. The causal order is therefore: miR-210 up → RISC loading → ISCU 3′UTR binding → reduced ISCU translation plus transcript destabilization → lower ISCU output (and consequently poorer Fe–S cluster assembly, the metabolic phenotype miR-210 is known to drive). Note this runs counter to the HIF1A→ISCU arm in your context: HIF1A raises miR-210 transcription, and the microRNA then sets a ceiling on ISCU, so the net direction under a miR-210 gain is downward.

NRIP1 is a direct ESR1 (ERα) target: liganded ERα binds estrogen-response elements in the NRIP1 promoter and drives its transcription. Because the perturbation is loss/reduction of NRIP1 itself, the transcript that is being measured is the one being removed — targeted knockdown or CRISPRi of NRIP1 lowers its own mRNA — and any secondary loop reinforces the same direction, since NRIP1 (RIP140) serves as an ERα cofactor whose depletion dampens ERα-dependent transcription of the same promoter. Order: NRIP1 loss → reduced NRIP1 transcript (and reduced ERα-driven NRIP1 promoter activity) → lower NRIP1 expression than the matched unperturbed control.

PPARα (PPARA) is a ligand-activated nuclear receptor that, upon activation, heterodimerizes with RXR and binds PPAR response elements (PPREs) in the promoters/enhancers of its target genes. *Angptl4* (fasting-induced adipose factor) carries a functional PPRE and is one of the best-characterized direct PPARα target genes — well documented in liver (and also via PPARβ/δ in other tissues). The causal order is therefore: PPARA activation → PPARα/RXR binding to the *Angptl4* PPRE → increased *Angptl4* transcription → higher Angptl4 mRNA (and secreted ANGPTL4 protein), which then acts as an LPL inhibitor. Because the effect is direct transcriptional activation rather than an indirect feedback arm, acute gain-of-function of PPARA raises *Angptl4* expression relative to the matched unperturbed control.

lincRNA-p21 (TP53COR1) sits downstream of p53: DNA damage or p53 activation induces it, and it then acts as a corepressor arm of the p53 response by binding hnRNP-K and recruiting it to the promoters of a subset of p53 target genes. Mtap4 is one of those genes — it appears in the set corepressed by p53, lincRNA-p21 and hnRNP-K, with hnRNP-K ChIP signal at its promoter that is lost when lincRNA-p21 is knocked down. So the causal order runs p53 → lincRNA-p21 → hnRNP-K loading at the Mtap4 promoter → transcriptional repression. Removing lincRNA-p21 severs that repressive arm while leaving the activating p53 input intact, so Mtap4 loses its hnRNP-K-dependent silencing and shifts to a de-repressed, higher-expression state relative to the matched control. Note this is a derepression effect, not direct activation — the magnitude depends on there being an active p53/hnRNP-K repressive tone in the context.

SMAD3 acts as a positive (activating) transcriptional regulator of PTPRK. After TGF-β stimulation, SMAD3 is phosphorylated by the TGF-β receptor complex, partners with SMAD4, and the SMAD3/SMAD4 complex binds a Smad-binding element (SBE) in the PTPRK promoter/enhancer, recruiting coactivators such as p300/CBP to drive transcription; Notch (via NICD–SMAD3 interaction) cooperates to further boost this induction. Loss or reduction of SMAD3 therefore removes the activating signal at the PTPRK locus, so PTPRK mRNA and protein fall (a reduction in basal and especially ligand-induced PTPRK expression) — which in turn releases EGFR/ErbB from PTPRK-mediated dephosphorylation. Causal order: SMAD3 loss → loss of SMAD3/SMAD4 occupancy and coactivator recruitment on the PTPRK regulatory element → reduced PTPRK transcription → lower PTPRK expression.

Perturbing that upstream regulatory site abolishes the OCT4 docking site, so the activating input at the enhancer is lost and enhancer–promoter communication to the Nanog promoter weakens. Order of events: regulatory-site perturbation → loss of POU5F1 binding → failure to assemble the activating complex/coactivator recruitment → reduced transcription initiation at the Nanog promoter → lower Nanog mRNA and protein relative to the matched unperturbed control. FOXK1 is not an activator of TP63 transcription — it is a required co-factor that p63 recruits to build the enhancer–promoter contacts it needs to switch on its target program. In the "secondary mode" of p63-dependent regulation, p63-bound enhancers reach the HNRNPA1 promoter only indirectly, through FOXK1-associated intermediate anchors, so the p63–FOXK1 pair must be intact for the loop to form. When FOXK1 is lost or knocked down, those p63-dependent loops selectively weaken while p63 protein levels themselves stay unchanged — the loss is architectural, not a drop in the transcription factor. The causal order is therefore: FOXK1 depletion → disassembly/weakening of the p63-dependent enhancer–promoter loop at the HNRNPA1 locus → loss of TP63-mediated transactivation at that promoter → reduced HNRNPA1 transcription. Because TP63's effect on HNRNPA1 is activating and FOXK1 is the limiting partner that enables it, the matched control comparison should show HNRNPA1 expression going **down**.

MAFG and MAFF are small Maf proteins that serve as obligate heterodimerization partners for NFE2L2 (NRF2); the NRF2 basic-leucine-zipper protein cannot bind DNA on its own, so it engages antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the Txnrd1 regulatory region only as an NRF2–sMaf heterodimer. Order of events: (1) MAFG/MAFF abundance is lowered by the perturbation, (2) the pool of NRF2–sMaf heterodimers available to recognize ARE sequences collapses, (3) NRF2 occupancy at the Txnrd1 ARE drops and its transactivation of the gene is lost, (4) Txnrd1 mRNA (and subsequently thioredoxin reductase 1 protein) declines relative to the matched unperturbed control. The key mediator is therefore the NRF2–sMaf heterodimer and ARE occupancy, not NRF2 protein level itself — NRF2 may even be stabilized/accumulated but is transcriptionally inert without its small Maf partner. This holds as net down despite the fact that small Mafs can also homodimerize on AREs and repress: in this context their dominant functional role is as the activating partner that NRF2 requires, so removing them reduces rather than de-represses Txnrd1 output. (Caveat: the direction assumes NFE2L2 is the active driver of Txnrd1 in this cell context; if NRF2 signaling is absent, the sMaf perturbation would have little effect.)

SNAP25 is a canonical neuronal gene whose promoter carries a RE1/NRSE element bound by REST, which silences it in non-neuronal and progenitor contexts. REST does not repress on its own — the repression depends on corepressor complexes, and the hSWI/SNF (BAF) chromatin-remodeling complex is a required component of the REST repressive machinery: BRG1/SMARCA4, the ATPase subunit, is recruited to REST-occupied promoters and its nucleosome-sliding activity, together with the associated HDAC activity, keeps the locus in a closed, deacetylated state. The order of events is therefore: BRG1 loss → BAF complex fails to assemble/act at REST target promoters → the REST–corepressor module (CoREST, HDACs, MeCP2-linked deacetylation) can no longer establish/maintain the repressed chromatin state, and REST occupancy and silencing capacity at these sites drop → the SNAP25 promoter becomes accessible with increased histone acetylation (H3K9ac/H3K27ac) → transcriptional de-repression. So the key mediator is loss of REST-dependent, BRG1-facilitated silencing, and SNAP25 expression rises relative to the matched control.

Hence expression goes down relative to the matched control.

LED (LncRNA activator of Enhancer Domains) sits downstream of TP53 in the same arm of the pathway: p53 binds a response element in the LED locus and drives its transcription, and LED then acts back on chromatin rather than on p53 itself. LED binds strong enhancer domains and promotes H3K9 acetylation there, one of its prominent targets being an enhancer within the CDKN1A gene. So the causal order is p53 → LED induction → LED-bound CDKN1A enhancer activation (increased eRNA and H3K9ac) → CDKN1A/p21 transcription. Reducing LED therefore removes a required co-activator: enhancer induction at CDKN1A fails, and p21 mRNA and protein both fall, while p53 levels themselves are unchanged (so this is not a p53-mediated effect but a loss of the downstream lncRNA-dependent enhancer step). Reported knockdown experiments in p53 wild-type breast cancer lines (MCF-7 and others) show exactly this — significantly reduced CDKN1A/p21 expression and a weakened G1 arrest — placing CDKN1A as the downstream readout and LED as its upstream enhancer-activating mediator.
